item.title: Combatting Loneliness via the Kindness of Strangers
item.description:
Loneliness

Combatting Loneliness via the Kindness of Strangers

Hanging with people you don't know is better than you may think.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Reaching out to someone you don't know can boost your mood.
  • Strangers are often more receptive to conversation than we expect.
  • You don’t have to start a conversation—a smile or holding a door open can also create a sense of connection.

It seems counterintuitive that someone you’ve never met can make you happy. But they can. Human beings evolved to seek connection as a basic means of survival in a hostile world. Things haven’t changed much since. In an ideal world, we’d quench our hunger for contact with a buffet of loving family members, friends, fringe-ships. But most of us don’t live in an ideal world. And loneliness is rampant.

On any given day, if you leave your house, you are likely to encounter a stranger. You know the cliché: A stranger is just a friend you haven’t met. Yeah, well, that’s just a cliché. Sure, you might make a new friend if you meet new people. But let’s not go overboard; a stranger is often just a stranger. But reaching out to “just a stranger” can boost your psychological well-being.

People who make small talk (e.g., “Nice weather”) with others in line or greet the barista report feeling more like they belong in that setting. Simply thanking someone, opening the door for the next person, and making eye contact can boost your mood.

Strangers can be surprisingly good sources of information. Try asking the checkout clerk at Trader Joe’s what they think about the frozen Thai dish—and you might get a tip that adding frozen spinach makes for a complete meal. Likewise, when people are experiencing distressing life circumstances such as a serious illness or a death in the family, a stranger with a similar experience might provide the most effective support. Friends and family are often too close to the problem, question their own ability to provide the right kind of help, or sometimes get a little pushy about knowing what’s right.

Most people expect encounters with strangers to be more awkward and less rewarding than they actually are. We also underestimate how much a stranger might benefit from the encounter. Other people are lonely, too, and your brief encounter might boost their mood. Research has found that sharing positive experiences with any social partner (close, acquaintance, or stranger) on a given day was associated with better mood and a stronger sense of resilience in the face of stress.

A Few Disclaimers

Maybe you’re a misanthrope. Or you’re an introvert. You’re the type of person who finds the idea of connecting with someone you don’t know aversive. You’d be fine staying home and watching YouTube videos. Well, sorry, you don’t get a break. Staying home alone or avoiding people isn't good for anyone. Research shows that introverts can benefit from talking to people as much (or more) than extroverts do. People prefer many things that aren’t good for them. Personally, I have been known to stop by See’s Chocolate for the free sample. Case in point.

You don’t have to talk to get the boost. If you’re not a chatty person, don’t chat. It is easy to share a brief moment of emotion with a stranger. Exchanging a smile can enhance mood. Or sharing your annoyance with someone else who just got splashed at the crosswalk by that car driving too fast through a puddle.

Then again, cultural norms might set up barriers to conversation. Here in Texas, you can ask a stranger buying flowers at the grocery store who they are giving them to and why, and learn all about their marital proposal (or just their anniversary). Perhaps you live in New York City, however, where it feels awkward to talk to strangers (and definitely weird on the subway). However, research shows that even on commuter trains in Chicago or London, people enjoyed talking with strangers more than they had expected. At the very least, giving up your seat can spark a connection.

This isn’t to say that everyone feels equally lonely or has equal access to strangers. People in rural areas often feel lonely but encounter fewer strangers in daily life. People from groups that face discrimination may have trouble getting a warm welcome from strangers in some settings. However, the benefits of brief contact with strangers are evident for individuals from diverse backgrounds and worth an effort.

Bottom Line

Talking with strangers isn’t difficult, and the more you do it, the easier it gets. One study created a scavenger hunt and asked people to run around for a week looking for strangers to talk with. By the end of the week, participants felt much less fearful of talking to people they didn’t know, felt better about their conversational abilities, and had an enhanced sense of their ability to connect with others. Win, win, win.

A new book (Once Upon a Stranger) offers QUICK as a mnemonic for a set of strategies to help you start a conversation. QU: Ask a question: Why are the four of you wearing polka-dotted skirts? (A colleague asked this question recently of a group of young women. Turns out they were going to an immersive Grease experience.) IC: Comment on something you have in common (e.g., Could this line be any slower?). K: Be kind and offer a sincere compliment (e.g., I love your pineapple earrings!).

Even if the stranger doesn’t engage, you benefit from the effort.

Smiling has a positive effect on mood, especially when it’s social; you feel happier because you smiled at someone.

Speaking aloud is a means of acknowledging yourself. It grounds you and makes you present, even if the conversation doesn’t pick up steam or extend.

To paraphrase the Beatles in their song about Eleanor Rigby: There are all kinds of lonely people. But brief social interactions can be transcendent. Strangers are an infinite resource; the world is filled with strangers.

Take this advice from a stranger: Go out there, smile, nod, and talk to people. Do it and do it often. You’ll like it more than you expect.

With gratitude to Gillian Sandstrom, Ph.D., for editorial comments.

item.title: How Christian Therapists Use Spirituality in Couples Therapy
item.description:
Religion

How Christian Therapists Use Spirituality in Couples Therapy

Encouraging hope, prayer, and forgiveness complement standard interventions.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • In this study, therapists integrated spirituality with established approaches to couples therapy.
  • Hope, prayer, forgiveness, and listening to the heart were the most common spiritual interventions.
  • Couples experienced meaningful reductions in spiritual, psychological, and relationship distress.
  • Therapists respected clients' spiritual preferences rather than imposing their own.
Source: Fizkes / Shutterstock / Used with permission

Today, I share additional findings from the Enhancing Practice-Based Evidence for Spiritually Integrated Psychotherapies project, focusing on a study of spiritually integrated couples therapy published in the APA journal Psychotherapy (Ripley et al., 2022). The findings offer valuable insights for psychotherapists seeking to incorporate spiritual interventions into their work with couples. I thank Dr. Jennifer Ripley for permission to share the study's findings.

Purpose of the Study

Spiritually incorporating couple therapy (SICT) has an expanding research base, yet relatively little is known about how therapists incorporate spirituality in routine clinical practice. Most previous studies have examined manualized treatments delivered in research settings rather than therapy as it naturally occurs in everyday practice. This study examined what actually occurs in SICT as practiced in clinical settings. SICT was defined as couples therapy that incorporates spiritual resources at the couple's request to address relationship concerns.

Research Design

The researchers used a practice-based evidence design to observe how therapists naturally integrated spirituality into their work. Using an online assessment system, the researchers collected treatment process and outcome data on 65 couples, 29 therapists, and 402 therapy sessions. Couples and therapists were asked to complete baseline and weekly session surveys for at least the first six sessions. Many couples voluntarily continued beyond six sessions. Therapists completed reports after each session detailing the therapeutic approaches used, the spiritual interventions employed, and the issues discussed during therapy. Clients completed repeated measures of psychological distress, relational distress, spiritual distress, marital satisfaction, relationship efficacy, and emotional forgiveness.

Participants

Therapists and couples were recruited from five large counseling facilities and solo practices in Virginia and North Carolina that advertise SICT as a practice approach. Among the couples, 81 percent were married, 11 percent were engaged, and 8 percent were in exclusive relationships without being married or engaged. Most clients (96 percent) identified as Christian; 94 percent said religion or spirituality was important in their lives, and 90 percent wanted religious or spiritual issues discussed in counseling when relevant. About one-third reported that religion or spirituality had contributed to some of their difficulties.

Of the therapists, 19 were female, and 10 were male; 18 were licensed clinicians, 11 were nonlicensed, and 11 were in practicum, internship, or residency. Of those licensed, 15 were counselors, two were psychologists, and one was a social worker. All therapists self-identified as Christian. Most engaged in individual spiritual disciplines, including daily prayer (91 percent) and scripture reading (55 percent).

Process Findings

Therapists generally did not use spirituality as a substitute for conventional couple therapy. Instead, they drew heavily on established therapeutic approaches and incorporated spiritual interventions when appropriate. Most therapists were theoretically eclectic. The most frequently used approaches were Hope-Focused Couple Therapy (50 percent of sessions), followed by Emotion-Focused Couple Therapy (36 percent), general spiritually integrated approaches (33 percent), general nonspecific approaches (28 percent), Christian counseling (20 percent), Solution-Focused Therapy (17 percent), and Gottman Couple Therapy (13 percent).

The spiritual interventions therapists used most frequently included discussing hope (55 percent of sessions), silently praying for the couple (46 percent), discussing forgiveness (30 percent), encouraging clients to listen to their hearts (30 percent), encouraging partners to pray (27 percent), discussing compassion (26 percent), and discussing self-control (26 percent). Therapists also frequently addressed other common emotional and relationship issues during sessions, including anger, love and affection, anxiety, coping, parenting, family-of-origin relationships, and infidelity.

Outcome Findings

Among the 32 couples who completed six sessions, there were significant reductions in psychological distress (d = .40; a small-to-medium effect size) and spiritual distress (d = .70; a medium-to-high effect size). Relational distress also decreased (d = .37; a small-to-medium effect size). These effect sizes are considered clinically meaningful. Other relationship measures—including marital satisfaction, emotional forgiveness, and relationship efficacy—did not show significant (statistical) improvement over six sessions. Thus, the couples showed some improvement, particularly in spiritual, psychological, and relational distress, but the evidence did not demonstrate substantial short-term changes on other measures.

Discussion

The study has important limitations. The sample was small and nonrandom; therapists were primarily from a limited geographic region, and almost all therapists and clients were Christian. Despite these limitations, the study provided valuable insights into the practice of spiritually integrated couple therapy in treatment settings that advertise SICT.

Couples’ spirituality influenced the use of spiritual interventions more than therapists’ spirituality did. When clients rated spirituality as more important, therapists were more likely to incorporate Christian or spiritual techniques. In contrast, therapists' own religious commitment and the frequency of their personal religious practices were not associated with their use of spiritual interventions. Thus, therapists generally followed the clients’ lead rather than imposing their own spiritual beliefs or practices. This is widely recognized as a foundation for ethical and effective spiritually integrated treatment (Pargament, 2011; Richards & Bergin, 2005; Richards et al., 2023).

It was also noteworthy that only 32 of the 65 religious couples completed six sessions. Couples who entered therapy with greater psychological distress, lower marital satisfaction, and less confidence in their ability to improve their relationship were more likely to terminate early. The researchers suggested that highly distressed Christian, and perhaps other religious, couples may constitute a population requiring particular attention early in treatment. They may enter therapy with diminished hope that their relationship can be repaired, making them especially vulnerable to discouragement and early termination.

It was also notable that the frequency with which therapists incorporated spiritual approaches did not significantly predict improvements in psychological, relational, or spiritual distress. Thus, the study showed that simply adding more spiritual interventions does not improve therapeutic outcomes, a finding consistent with other studies (e.g., Sanders et al., 2015).

Conclusions

The study found that couples who completed at least six sessions experienced clinically meaningful improvements in spiritual, psychological, and relationship distress. This evidence supports the effectiveness of spiritually integrated couple therapy grounded in established couple-therapy practices. The researchers emphasized the importance of respecting clients' preferences, using evidence-based couple approaches, and paying particular attention to highly distressed religious couples, who may be at greater risk of leaving therapy prematurely. They also recommended further research examining how spiritually integrated couple therapy is practiced and how it influences long-term outcomes.

item.title: Your Phone Should Work for You, Not Against You
item.description:
Executive Function

Your Phone Should Work for You, Not Against You

Three ways to build executive functioning by organizing your apps.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Executive functioning isn’t just about knowing what to do but also about being able to get to it.
  • It's important to decrease the distance between intention and action.
  • Organizing apps on devices can take students from "I have to do this" to actually getting it done.

For students with ADHD who struggle with executive functioning, getting started and staying focused can be just as difficult as completing the task itself. Notifications, endless scrolling, and searching for apps can create distractibility and overwhelm before a child even begins their work. The goal is to have an idea about a task or assignment that needs to be completed and to be able to access it easily and quickly while the momentum and motivation are there.

I recently worked with a young man to reorganize his phone, putting the most frequently accessed apps on the home screen and grouping others into folders. The goal was to make accessing information easier so he could spend less time searching and more time getting work done.

During our executive functioning coaching session, here are the three things that he and I discovered.

Make getting started easier

This young man shared with me that he would like to read his college email more frequently but often can’t find the app itself. At other times, he can’t remember the login. Students who struggle with task initiation benefit from having fewer steps between sitting down to work and beginning. Organizing the phone's home screen to feature frequently used school apps, calendars, and to-do lists is helpful and creates less of a delay in starting. Making clearly labeled folders for apps is one way to create space for the apps.

Apply the same strategy to the computer. Keep essential school apps and shortcuts together on the desktop, in a central location where the student naturally looks. The fewer steps required to find what they need, the easier it is to begin.

Reduce distractions and overwhelm

For students who are easily distracted, notifications and having to search through multiple screens can redirect their attention before they even start working. Teenagers and young adults are encouraged to turn off notifications for all apps (except for one or two where that notification is useful). I encourage students to go into an app when they want to check email or texts but not have the information come to them—they can go to it. Focus or Do Not Disturb settings are also very helpful during homework time, and move entertainment apps away from the main home screen.

Keep important apps visible and accessible so looking for an app doesn’t become a chore in and of itself. By the time your student navigates to the actual app, he or she may not remember what they were looking for to begin with. Reducing visual clutter and interruptions can help them maintain attention and avoid feeling overwhelmed by too much information.

Externalize memory and build independence

With all of the information that needs to be remembered about logins and passwords for different apps, there is no way that can be held in memory. Students are encouraged to place passwords in (password-protected) notes, use folders for schoolwork with clear labels, and create reminders and alarms for assignments and deadlines.

Allowing the young man I was working with to create the organizational system for his apps that made the most sense to him gave him control over his phone and computer screen. I asked him to explain his mindset and rationale; as he shared his organizational system and the reasoning behind it, he seemed proud of himself. He even shared that he felt accomplished as he was leaving our session.

While working with this young man, I realized that we weren’t just organizing apps. We were creating a space for him to decrease the obstacles that get in the way of him getting started, minimizing distractions and building his independence and pride.

item.title: Disenfranchised Grief: When a Friend Dies
item.description:
Friends

Disenfranchised Grief: When a Friend Dies

The loss of a friend in later life issues in a special, little understood grief.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • When we grieve for a friend who has died, we face multiple concerns.
  • For older people, the loss of a long-term friend means we have lost a life witness.
  • We sometimes grieve for the loss of a difficult friendship because not every good friendship is easy.

There is a special kind of grief when, in older life, a longtime friend dies. The grief is complicated by its lack of place in the norms of mourning, sometimes called "disenfranchised grief" because friends are not formally recognized as mourners.[1]

Many years ago I wrote a book about friendships with Ruthellen Josselson in which we delved into the pains and pleasures of female friendships across the lifespan.[2] One important theme girls spoke about was loss. Young girls lose friends as yesterday’s best friend gravitates to another buddy or as a confidant reveals a secret behind her back. Women lose friends through uneasy competition and conflict and a sense of betrayal, while some friendships simply melt away as we move to a different city or become absorbed in new duties and demands.

In a recent conversation with Ruthellen, she reflected on how our relative youth at the time of writing blinded us to a significant element in friendship: the loss we suffer when a friend dies. My own recent experiences have challenged me to focus on this topic.

The Many Faces of Grief

Grief at the death of a friend has many different aspects. There is sadness via empathy. I feel sad for my friend, for the pain she might have endured throughout the last months of life and for her unspent productivity. I feel sad for her partner, to whom I also feel attached, as he now faces an echoing absence when he wakes, when he sleeps, when he walks, and when he thinks. I also feel sad for myself because I have lost a companion and "someone to talk to."

Since we construct friends as "like us" via our affinity with them, their death thins the border between living and not living. It seems so easy, now, to pass into non-life, that my sentience, however vivid at the moment, is porous and frail.

The Special Grief in Later Life

Long-term friends also offer something else more difficult to define. My sense of loss at the death of a friend I have known since childhood might puzzle others: "You rarely saw her or spoke to her; why is her death affecting you so deeply?"

This seems like a reasonable question but ignores the unique place a decades-old friendship provides as a witness to one’s life, with its inevitable shifts, disappointments, and solaces. Nothing can replace the intimate history and meanings provided by friendship’s longevity.

Moreover, those in their 70s and 80s are likely to experience the loss of more than one friend within the span of a few years. Each new loss constricts their social world, and older people are likely to feel they have fewer opportunities for making new friends. As research repeatedly shows, older people’s well-being—both physical and mental—is highly correlated with the level of their social connections.

Grief Even for the Loss of a Difficult Friendship

Another puzzle about such disenfranchised grief is that its intensity is not eased just because the friendship was difficult. Recently I lost someone with whom my relationship did not fit the standard friendship box. The mismatch between my panic at the loss of this friend on the one hand, and the nature of our friendship on the other, leads me to re-think some very basic assumptions about good friendships.

This was not an easy relationship. She was very direct in her speech and not always on my side. Often, after time spent with her, I had to recalibrate my vanity, shaken by her brusque observations. A quasi-public debate in which I thought I had triumphed was judged by her to be no more than "a draw." When I showed her a manicure in the expectation of admiration, she commented on my arthritic finger with a vehemence—"How awful!"—that sounded like a reprimand. When I spoke to her about my distress over the divorce of someone close to me, her intellect trounced empathy, and sliced into my vulnerability with the brutal remark, "I wonder what an objective view [of who’s at fault] would be."

My attachment to her sometimes wobbled but never toppled. Throughout the lockdowns and restrictions of the COVID-19 pandemic, we exchanged emails and set up video calls that provided a welcome soundboard for my thoughts about the very strange new world around us. From time to time, she expressed impatience with what she called my "mini-lectures"—my attempts to compress ideas so they could be refined or endorsed through conversation, but the reassurance I had in sharing my thoughts with her was a sufficient counterweight to her criticisms.

I wonder whether I will be able to navigate life's last act without her, unprotected and undirected by this shrewd and opinionated woman.

The Notion of a Sandpaper Friendship

As Ruthellen and I wrote Best Friends, we puzzled over why girls so often refused to end an uncomfortable friendship. "Why do you want to be friends with her?" we heard their mothers demand. "You know she’s not nice to you?" The loss of this friend helps me understand those young girls in a new way.

Comfort and acceptance are indeed among the joys of friendship, but there are other building blocks of friendship. Close contact with a mind and personality that disturbs our equilibrium can be interesting and worthwhile, even when it doesn’t fit the mold of a perfect friendship. In Best Friends, Ruthellen and I concluded that girls’ friendships were notoriously volatile because they idealized a "best friend" as someone who is unerringly kind, admiring, and supportive, where any deviation from the positive falls into the category of "bad friend." My reaction to this friendship loss has introduced me to the notion of a sandpaper friendship, where we might feel a little raw after rubbing together but also feel more real and more resilient, knowing we can navigate an uneven friendship.

item.title: Should You Forgive? How One Novel Answers That Question
item.description:
Forgiveness

Should You Forgive? How One Novel Answers That Question

Author Imbolo Mbue explores the complexities of guilt and forgiveness in her latest novel.

Posted October 6, 2026

Unforgiveness can be protective. No one wants to get hurt again when wronged by someone else, and it feels morally just that the wrongdoer should suffer in some way for what they’ve done.

Yet research has shown that holding a grudge can be detrimental to our health and wellbeing. It activates our sympathetic nervous system, putting us into fight-or-flight, increasing anxiety, causing us to lose sleep, and increasing our chances of dying from any cause. The negativity we carry when we refuse to forgive can eat away at us, from the inside out (Why Forgiveness Is Good for Your Health, 2026).

Forgiveness is not about absolution. According to forgiveness scholar Everett Worthington at Virginia Commonwealth University, forgiving someone is about what is going on inside of you. It is defined by catching negative thoughts, emotions, and behaviors toward the person who hurt you, and consciously choosing to replace them with positive thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. It’s about setting down the burden of negativity and choosing to embody positivity – for your own wellbeing.

Author Imbolo Mbue crafted a masterful, layered story of guilt, the complexities of right and wrong, forgiveness, and love in her latest novel Every Story is a Love Story. Mbue’s moving story is universal, deeply human, and a compelling reminder that we all are faced with the difficult task of forgiving – and being forgiven.

Q: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write Every Story is a Love Story.

Imbolo Mbue: I grew up in a beautiful seaside town called Limbe, Cameroon. Mine was a childhood full of stories and fascinating characters but I never imagined I'd grow up to write stories. Interesting, though, a lot of my storytelling is shaped by events that happened in Limbe. This particular novel was inspired by an event that happened when I was a teenager—I was involved in a fight that left a young man injured and with a scar on his face. At the time I didn't think much about the incident but many years later, something about the pandemic brought back the memory of that fight and I felt terrible for the young man and his mother, who had to tend to her bleeding child. I never intended to write about guilt but a novel I was working on wasn't quite coming together so I took a character from that novel and began writing this story.

Q: In your book, how does sudden, traumatic loss shape Wolo’s life? In what ways is he changed by this loss?

Imbolo Mbue: I'm not sure anyone can be unchanged by what befell Wolo. He goes from nearly having it all to being terribly lost and alone. Thoughts and feelings he was not accustomed to managing on a daily basis replaced his comfortable, optimistic mindset. And not only did he have to face his own internal thoughts, he was forced to contend with how his mother, father-in-law, pastor and wider circle in the Cameroonian community reacted to the tragedy.

The loss was primarily his but it wasn't only his, and the decision on how to treat the person who accidentally killed his wife wasn't only his either. That was another burden he had to bear.

Q: In what ways do you think forgiveness plays a powerful role in our lives? How might Wolo’s story have been different without forgiveness?

Imbolo Mbue: Over the years, several friends have shared with me their struggles to forgive or not to forgive, how to forgive, how to get forgiveness from others. We can't escape that battle. As long as we live we will hurt and be hurt by others and forgiveness will sooner or later enter the equation. What we choose to do is so individual, it has so much to do with our unique ways of seeing the world and the values we live by. Wolo's struggle with the decision is very different from his mother's because even though they both loved Yoma thoroughly, they are very different humans and their hearts are different.

Source: Penguin Random House/Used with permission

Q: How can “every story be a love story” in our own lives? How might literature help readers to choose love, and make the world a better place?

Imbolo Mbue: Love has the ability to slide into any circumstance, like water. It's as if we are all on a constant search for love—romantic love, platonic love, familial love, love from strangers on the internet.

Personally, I think when we are guided by the desire to reach out and connect with another human, it is not difficult for every story to become a love story in our lives. Perhaps in some stories it is near impossible to see the love present, especially when there's an incredible amount of wickedness or injustice, but love has the ability to seep into the darkest of situations and we end up seeing light in a story that on the surface appears to have nothing to do with love.

That, I believe, is the beauty of literature--its power to take readers to places where they can find light and love in darkness.

Q: What do you hope readers take away from spending time with Every Story is a Love Story?

Imbolo Mbue: I started writing this story without a true appreciation of how difficult forgiveness is. By the time I finished writing it, I had developed a whole lot of empathy for people who refuse to forgive. And I am in awe of those who are able to forgive what can easily be called unforgivable. I don't believe either is necessarily an easy choice.

The least I can do, I've decided, is show compassion for all who are on a forgiveness journey.

item.title: When Things Between Mom and Dad Are Bad: What to Say
item.description:
Parenting

When Things Between Mom and Dad Are Bad: What to Say

Kids sense when parents are upset. It's best to not leave them wondering why.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Kids sense when parents are having a hard time. Without real information, they worry and can blame themselves.
  • Facing up to a conversation can be very daunting to a parent since it means confronting their own upset.
  • Thinking through what you can say, and what you shouldn't share, is really the key to this complex situation.

Kids sense things about you, even when you don't say anything, just as you sense things about them. Maybe because they come from you and have learned to understand and communicate with you through a nonverbal intimacy, they can tell when things feel off. So, kids really know when something serious is going on without being told.

Even though it probably feels to you like the reckoning from hell, the actual conversation about what they sense is “off” can be quite relieving for your child. A child knowing something, but feeling that they have to keep it to themselves is one of the most damaging things that can happen in childhood. More likely than not, a child in this position starts to make up reasons as a way of understanding all the differences they see and feel and, often, lacking other understanding, begins to blame themselves for what they sense is going on with their parents.

Margie noticed that Stevie was being uncharacteristically snappy with his sister and generally gloomy at home. This was what tipped her off that something was awry and led Margie to call for help. At school, teachers reported that Stevie was staying more to himself and was not showing his usual interest or focus. One teacher asked her, “Was anything going on at home?” Could Stevie have overheard Margie and her husband arguing about how much time they spent with his parents?

From our experience with families, this kind of behavioral change is not an unusual pattern when a child feels that something serious is going on within their family but doesn’t have information or confirmation. When your child’s behavior indicates that they can't bring something up with you, maybe because they are concerned with how you will feel or respond, you have reached a point where you need to show them your concern. It is constructive, even if difficult, to bring the painful subject up with them. And equally destructive to pretend that nothing is wrong. Your child’s behavior indicates that they sense something is not right and that this is burdening them. How you bring it up, when you bring it up, and what you say and don't say, is all very important to think through.

What Is It You Are Feeling?

How you are feeling has a strong impact on how you operate as a parent. It is why we always recommend that you work out your big feelings away from your child before you approach them with conversation. Seeing you upset will upset them. Just as it is not helpful to expose your child to marital arguments and strong displays of emotion, it is not good to bring strong emotions into conversations with your child. Once settled enough that you can feel self-control and hold a vision of yourself being capable of managing your emotions in front of your child, it is good to bring the issue up. It takes a great deal of reflection, self-talk, and confidence to sit down with your child to talk about something painful going on between you and your spouse. Many parents try to avoid such conversations because they can't tolerate the thought that they are responsible for creating something upsetting for their child. And sometimes, this can be as painful, or even more difficult, than the spousal problem itself.

How to Bring It Up

We have always found it best to find a quiet time in a private space, free from distractions, when having an emotional conversation with your child. If both parents have their feelings under control and are able to participate, it is beneficial for children to see their parents together, even though they may come to understand that their parents are having disagreements with each other. You might say, "As you have noticed, Mommy and Daddy have been having some arguments recently, but we want you to know it is just because we both have strong feelings about what we are talking about. That happens sometimes for all of us, even grownups.” Then you can ask if they have noticed and what they have been thinking/feeling about it. The point is to help them give voice to what they have experienced, help them to realize that what is going on between the grownups is not their fault and that sometimes parents argue, no matter how much they love each other.

If you do have to reveal very difficult news, do so when the timing is right and necessary. Tell only as much of the truth as necessary and help your child, in soothing tones, take in the hard news. But, on the other hand, if matters are being constructively and productively handled between you and your spouse, you can speak about how well you both feel talking things out together. This is not a one-time conversation. Stay very open to signs and signals after this conversation and always express your interest in hearing from them.

What to Say and What Not to Say

If your child asks you directly what you are arguing about, be very reassuring and tell them it is grown-up business and something just between Mommy and Daddy. Most importantly, prompt and listen to questions or comments stimulated by your conversation. Be as honest as you can to promote a sense of optimism, but don't detail the content of this adult business. A child should never be a confidant. They should leave a conversation relieved, not burdened.

Always keep in mind that you are not having this conversation to tell them details about what they may have overheard, thought they overheard, or imagine they understood. You are having the conversation to release the pressure they have put on themselves by feeling they cannot talk to you about something that they sense is wrong. You want to relieve them of the burden of any imagined guilt they may feel about being the source of a problem. And you want to establish clearly that you are available and open to them talking freely to you about whatever they sense, think, or feel, even about you.

Remember, they are reading you, even as they might misconstrue what they are reading. They know they are reading “something.” You don't want to speak more optimistically or pessimistically than what they witness between you, which is why you want to anchor your comments in their questions or observations. Never dissuade your child from bringing you their concerns, even though they might upset you. Always try to keep yourself reasonably upbeat, but not phony when speaking with your child. False optimism, pretending that everything is just dandy when your child senses it is not, will undercut your encouragement of openness and undercut your child’s trust in you. But honestly acknowledging that disagreement exists makes it less scary and threatening, especially if it is couched in an equally honest assessment that sometimes this happens and people can work it out. Acknowledging that they are not wrong in sensing some tension between their parents helps build and maintain trust because it shows your child that you can be trusted to be truthful.

As we have learned as clinicians, and as regular people ourselves, there are moments that arise in intimate partnerships that can be upsetting. We learn how to take in our hurts, disappointments, and disagreements and carry them. We learn to conduct ourselves appropriately in light of or in spite of those feelings. That means that good people can disagree and get upset with each other and compromise or find a way to move forward. Tension can dissipate with conversation. Resolutions can be reached. How we do this is the model our children can best learn from.

item.title: A Timeline of Emotional Labor
item.description:
Emotional Labor

A Timeline of Emotional Labor

Women have long been expected to manage everyone’s emotions.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional labor is the invisible work of managing one's feelings in order to shape someone else’s.
  • From alewives to assistants, women have long absorbed the emotional work their jobs don’t name.
  • Today the tools have changed, but the expectation to quietly absorb everyone’s emotions remains.

Picture a tiny tavern in the middle of a medieval forest. The tavern owner’s wife is watching her customers for refills, while soothing the broken heart of the local stable boy. She navigates the raised voices in the back of the room, knowing that fists can start swinging at a moment’s notice. If a job description existed, “reading the room” wouldn’t be listed as a “demonstrated ability. Her job was the ale. Everything else — recognizing a broken heart and stopping a bar fight — was invisible to all but the alewife. The work is still invisible. We just call it something different now, and mostly, we still don't pay for it.

Since time began, the gap between what a job description says and what a job requires of a person's inner life is what sociologist Arlie Hochschild named "emotional labor" in her 1983 book The Managed Heart. Hochschild studied flight attendants who were hired to serve drinks and make sure passengers followed safety procedures. But these professionals were also trained to manufacture their emotions to ensure their passengers felt the care, and regardless of whether the passenger was kind, hostile, or downright rude. Hochschild found that flight attendants (practically all women at the time) learned to fake a smile long enough for a living but eventually stopped being able to tell when their smile was real. They learned to manage their *own* internal state to produce a specific state in someone else.

Calling this learned behavior “emotional labor,” Hochschild shows us that this mostly invisible labor doesn't show up on an org chart or a job description. The reality is that most jobs in which women dominate (think teachers, nurses, social workers, domestic workers, and anyone in the care economy) incorporate these unpaid but almost rigidly expected patterns of behavior, namely, to always smile and keep anyone from knowing how you really feel.

We started with the alewife, which tells us that the management of feelings to make others around feel comfortable, is centuries older than the term. Tracing it — from the tavern to the cubicle to your inbox right now — shows how consistent the pattern is, and how much it costs the people carrying it. Here are some examples throughout history:

  • Domestic service, 1700s–1800s. Household labor performed by women hired by women, to do the tasks commonly known as ‘women’s work.’ I’m thinking of ladies' maids and governesses managing not only those tasks for which they were particularly hired for, but let’s face it, ear to the ground, they were also very aware of the emotional temperature of the households they worked in. They soothed the anxiety of their mistress, while keeping peace among the children who weren't theirs. The job title covered the physical parts of the work, and never included the invisible emotional layer of work associated with being present on the job.

  • In the early to mid-1900s, beginning with World War I when men left offices and factories to fight in Europe. Women dominated these workspaces in their wake, but with an interesting twist. With the white-collar ethos of moving up the corporate ladder (a young associate could expect his boss to show him the ropes), the emergence of women in these same spaces saw white-collar jobs migrate into pink-collar occupations. Not only were women typing memos, but they also picked up the dry cleaning and birthday gifts for bosses’ wives. As offices expanded, the secretary became the buffer between the boss and the world. To keep things running smoothly, she learned how to ‘manage up’ and to do it well, making him look good without ever being credited for how.

  • Hochschild names it in 1983. Along with flight attendants, her research included bill collectors. Yes, bill collectors who were successful when they didn’t show any emotion listening to debtors' sad stories about why they couldn’t pay their debt. Where flight attendants manufacture kindness and warmth, bill collectors had to manufacture cold detachment. Hochschild called this managing of one feeling to produce an emotional state emotional labor, and for first time in our long 'herstory,' the invisible work had a name.

  • Burnout goes mainstream, 2010s. In the decade before COVID, the concept and language of ‘emotional labor’ goes mainstream. Women are finding platforms to talk about and commiserate over the ever-growing, never-ending, always-something-coming-up volume of work for wives and mothers, adult daughters and caregivers. Academics wrote books calling out the lack of gender equity. Journalists posted blogs and articles attesting to burnout and frustration and the acknowledgement that there simply was not enough Calgon on the planet to take them away. Take them away from what? At home: being the one who remembers the pediatrician's number, notices when a friend goes quiet, manages everyone's feelings about the family dinner, and knows where to locate the missing sock. At work: planning the office parties, sending around bereavement cards for everyone to sign, mentoring new employees. All of these ways in which we show our kindness and humanity are lovely — and the unwritten job scope widens and follows you everywhere.

  • Today. You're managing a Slack channel's tone, while an anxious client is on hold. You’re spending more hours at the office and experiencing a parent's guilt trip, and your own exhaustion. And all this is happening in the same hour. The tools have changed. The expectation that someone will quietly absorb the emotional weather of a room has not.

item.title: The Thing About Things: Self-Expression and Belonging
item.description:
Identity

The Thing About Things: Self-Expression and Belonging

How belonging and self-expression bring us back to ourselves.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Belonging offers safety, but without agency, it can leave a person secure and still unsure of who she is.
  • Women are skilled at compromise, and over time compromise can cost us our own point of view.
  • Our wardrobe is an expression of identity and may be where we first notice we have lost track of ourselves.

By Stacy Feiner and Roberta Style Lee

Nearly €100,000 of clothing sat in Nicole's closets in her London flat, most of it still folded in boutique bags.

Through each career change, her mother offered the same reassurance: “Nicole, you don't have to work, sweetheart. You're taken care of.” Friends and family repeated versions of this as well. It was meant lovingly—but it made her feel small. Gradually, she started to believe it. If she was taken care of, what was left for her to pursue? What value did she bring?

Children need to know they are safe in the world. They need to know they are not alone, that they will not go hungry, get lost, or be forgotten. That sense of security is part of belonging. Nicole had it in abundance.

What she had less of was the other part of belonging: the confidence to pursue an interest, accomplish a goal, contribute something of value, and experience herself as someone who could make things happen. Families that do well across generations cultivate security while encouraging agency (Wolkowitz & Feiner, 2025).
For Nicole, agency had gradually become optional.

Her family found real meaning in providing for her, and their care was genuine. But care that required nothing from her gave her no place to discover what she could contribute. Healthy relational connection provides an experience that is rewarding to each person, even when it is rewarding in different ways, as it is between a parent and child (Miller, 1976). Nicole was being cared for, but she was not being recognized for what she could contribute. Over time, she internalized the message. Her confidence in her own capacity thinned, and she settled into an indifference that made it harder to know what she wanted, let alone act.

How Women Use Compromise and Autopilot to Cope

Women are profoundly good at using compromise to survive. We go into autopilot for a surprising amount of time, years, decades even.

Nicole felt that misalignment and dismissed it. Over time, she began to notice something was amiss. A person who cannot trust herself will start to seek validation from others.

Her move to London was a hopeful step that she might discover the spark in herself. Soon after her move, she began volunteering at a hospital, holding newborns and supporting new mothers. The work mattered to her and filled her days while the larger question of who she was remained open.

Which brings us back to Nicole’s closet.

Strolling through boutiques was a way to get out, meet people. More than shopping, she found it provided a sense of belonging.

At each boutique, the sales associates welcomed her, remembered her, and validated her needs. Knowing nothing about her, or who she might become, Nicole accepted their attention as connection and care. Her own self-worth was so thin she mistook the transaction for something more. By the time she returned home, the feeling faded. But the pleasure of the experience was just enough to send her back. Nicole thought she was shopping for clothes. She was shopping for the feeling of being seen.

Anyone who advises families of wealth has seen some version of this, whether it is an untouched fortune in a glass cabinet or any number of external relationship substitutes. Relational connection is what keeps a human system healthy, whether a family, a team, or an enterprise (Andreasson et al., 2023), and when a person's relational well-being goes missing, it is sought elsewhere. It gets revealed as unexpected spending at the portfolio review, or as tension in a family meeting that gets blamed on temperament, and because none of it is immediately noticed on a balance sheet, it tends to be addressed only once the costs start to accumulate.

How Clothing Choices Reflect and Shape Identity

For many people, clothes shopping is an effective endorphin release—a joy that quickly descends into wardrobe mayhem if left unchecked. Clothing has historically been a way to communicate who we are, yet the choices we make are too often guided by opinions and beliefs of others, and rarely our own. The closet becomes evidence of our past, misguided direction, and even aspirations never fulfilled. It can be confronting to deal with, but it also offers us the opportunity to reconnect with ourselves and who we want to be.

Every day getting dressed reinforces who we are to ourselves and the world. Positive self-expression from style comes from understanding what makes us unique, along with self-acceptance and alignment.

Nicole came to those questions by seeking guidance. Rather than beating herself up for owning too much, she began questioning how she wanted to feel in each piece. Eventually, she opened the bags. Some things she kept because they turned out to be hers; others she let go to make room for who she was to become.

Her time at the hospital changed as well. What had begun as a way to fill her days became something she pursued on purpose. She became someone the staff relied on, and found a connection that saw value and meaning in what she had to offer.

She was contributing to the lives around her and discovering herself through what she was able to give. Through it, she was recovering a relationship with herself, the capacity to notice what she felt, trust what she valued, and act on it, and with it a way of belonging that no longer required her to shop to be noticed.

Self-expression became part of that recovery.

The clothes were not simply a reflection of who Nicole was becoming. They gave her permission to explore parts of herself. In choosing what felt like her, rejecting what did not, and allowing herself to be seen on her own terms, she was discovering something about herself that could not have been found through reflection alone.

What she wore became part of the process of knowing who she was, what mattered to her, and how she wanted to experience the world. Each choice says something about how we see ourselves and how we wish to be seen, understood, and remembered.

Having things settles the question of need. Self-expression gives us another way to discover what matters to us, to make it visible, and to experience the power of seeing ourselves more clearly.

Roberta Lee, founder of Roberta Style Lee, is a style and identity expert specializing in identity, values, and personal presence. She works with women entering new chapters, using style as a tool to help them reconnect with themselves.

item.title: The Peril of Diseases Shared Between Animals and Humans
item.description:
Climate Anxiety

The Peril of Diseases Shared Between Animals and Humans

Michael Dulaney's book "Sentinels" examines zoonotic diseases.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Roughly three out of every four new diseases in humans come from animals.
  • Using the latest science, Dulaney writes about the fear of contagion and why we must do something about it.
  • It stresses the interconnectivity of all life on our planet and there's no free ride because we're special.
  • Human destruction of the environment is responsible for the accelerating spillover of animal diseases.
Source: Julian david/Pexels

Over the past few years, I have noticed an increasing number of scientific papers and news reports about the ever-increasing concern of diseases passed from nonhuman animals (animals) to humans. The spread of zoonotic diseases should be a concern to all of us, not only scientists who study them and physicians who treat them. That is one reason I am strongly drawn to the new, highly acclaimed book Sentinels: When Diseases Spread Between Animals and Humans by award-winning writer Michael Dulaney. In the book, he writes about "the interconnected forces of climate change, habitat destruction, factory farming, globalization, and inequality." If you're going to read one book on this alarming plight, this is the one.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Sentinels?

Michael Dulaney: The book explores how humans' impact on the environment is causing more infectious diseases to leap from animals to humans than ever before. I started researching the subject during the COVID-19 pandemic, when I discovered that scientists had been issuing eerily prescient warnings about just such a virus for many years prior. I was surprised to learn that most new diseases in humans come from animals, with human activity and exploitation of the natural world as the main cause. It was clearly an environmental story of global importance, one that will become more urgent as the climate crisis deepens.

Before I started writing the book, Australia suffered one of its worst bushfire seasons in history. For weeks, I walked to work through smoky streets with ash and blackened leaves raining down around me. I experienced the most intense eco-anxiety of my life. Writing about the environmental origins of infectious disease united those two urgent concerns (climate crisis and disease spillover) and it allowed me to examine how animals and humans are confronting these enormous changes.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

MD: I’ve written about humanity’s close links with animals for most of my career, and I’ve always tried to find unexpected ways to tell those environmental stories. Tracing the origins of infectious disease is a morbid topic; however, it is also fascinating and offers a unique entry point that explores bigger stories about animals, humans, and the climate crisis. These can reveal overlooked histories, ideas and relationships, saying much about how societies are organised. My reporting for the book took me around the world, and introduced me to many fascinating animal species, as well as the dedicated people working alongside them. I met people who care for sick and injured flying foxes in their homes, and talked with scientists studying tiny voles on the Alaskan tundra. I was lucky to visit the Indonesian mountains with conservationists caring for critically endangered frogs, and spend time with dedicated bird-watchers catching ducks to track the global spread of bird flu.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

MD: I’m hoping that Sentinels speaks to those who are curious about the natural world, and who also have a political belief that we need to build a fairer world for all kinds of life on this planet. Most of all, as a narrative journalist, I hope to reach people who love good stories.

Source: Scribe/with Permission

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

MD: The book explores how humans and non-human animals are navigating a shared (and increasingly volatile) future. Each chapter is its own story, covering a different animal species in a different part of the world, and it looks at a particular infectious disease as the starting point. It It examines stories about human society and ecological change. For example, the first chapter follows wildlife carers in Australia who take injured flying foxes into their homes. The chapter uses the origins of the Hendra virus to examine deforestation and global warming on the future of this flying mammal species.

Another chapter looks at how the enormous legal wildlife trade has reshaped ecosystems and spread disease around the world. Other chapters examine farming, land use changes, and issues in major cities. Of course, I had many close encounters with animals. I bottle-fed a tiny rehabilitated baby bat and held a critically endangered Indonesian frog, one of only a few dozen left in the wild. This brought home one of the book's major messages: Our fate is tied with theirs.

I also spent a lot of time with people doing this kind of repair work every day, in big and small ways; people who have given their lives to helping animals and their fellow humans, or to making the future better without any hope they would live to see it bear fruit. It left me feeling hopeful that this unheralded work is happening all over the world every day.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

MD: Sentinels uses diseases to explore much larger stories about this new planetary condition. Each chapter points to a broader, ominous social reality that is becoming ever more important to understand. It covers many subjects not immediately obvious as being related to disease, including affordable housing, incarceration and the pet trade. Most of all, it links these diseases to capitalism, an economic system that takes the whole of biological life and turns it into a machine for extracting maximum value—the very same force driving mass extinction and the climate crisis. The book highlights that no pharmaceutical fix can right this planetary health problem. The struggle for one equals the struggle for all.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about this topic they will pay more attention to this relationship and try to fix it?

MD: After writing Sentinels, I’ve been really encouraged with how many people say they want to get involved in whatever way they can. Some are dedicating their lives to repairing ecosystems or nursing endangered species back to health, or trying to understand the natural world to protect it. While we face enormous challenges in the climate crisis, millions of people want to do this work. And that makes me hopeful.

item.title: The Real Difference Between Living Longer and Living Better
item.description:
Aging

The Real Difference Between Living Longer and Living Better

What longevity science says about living a longer, healthier life.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Living longer is only part of the goal; healthspan matters, too.
  • The basics still matter. Sleep, physical activity, health checks, and relationships all play a role.
  • Focus on what you can control. Small, consistent changes can make a difference over time.
Source: Niko Hems / Used With Permission

Longevity has become a hot topic in recent years. There are many products on the market—for instance, supplements, wearable devices, cold plunges, fasting, and other ways people are trying to live longer and stay healthier. With the market saturated with information, it can be difficult to know what is actually supported by research and what may simply be another wellness trend.

To better understand what longevity science tells us, I spoke with Niko Hems, head of strategy and medical communications at YEARS, a Berlin-based physician-led preventive health clinic. His work focuses on preventive health and longevity and provides a useful perspective on what people should consider when thinking about their long-term health.

1. Think About Healthspan, Not Just Lifespan

When people say they want to live longer, they often mean that they want to remain healthy while they are living longer. This is where the concept of healthspan becomes important. Healthspan refers to the years a person spends in good health without significant disease or disability.

Experts note that lifespan and healthspan are not the same. For instance, data from 183 countries found that the United States had a 12.4-year gap between lifespan and healthspan. The researchers define this gap as the portion of life expectancy affected by disease or disability.

As Hems explained, “We talk about longevity as if the goal is to add more years. The actual goal is to still be the person you want to be for as long as possible. For many people, the goal is not simply to reach a certain age. It is to still be able to do the things that matter to them while maintaining the physical and mental functioning needed to live the life they want."

2. Start With the Basics

When thinking about how longevity may look, it can be easy to focus on the newest supplement, technology, or biohacking strategy. However, experts note that the strongest evidence continues to point toward more basic health behaviors.

For instance, it may sound simple, but physical movement, or behavioral activation, is consistently associated with lower mortality risk. Research has linked higher cardiorespiratory fitness with a lower risk of death. Maintaining strength and muscle also helps us stay physically capable and independent as we get older.

3. Know Your Health Numbers

Next, having a deeper understanding of our physiology is essential. Some health conditions can develop without obvious symptoms. Having data on our biomarkers, blood pressure, blood glucose, cholesterol, and other health markers can provide information about our health before we notice a problem. This allows us to be proactive instead of reactive. The goal is not to constantly monitor every number but instead to understand which measures are meaningful for you.

4. Pay Attention to Sleep

Sleep is another basic behavior that can play an important role in long-term health. Although we may already know this, many of us do not get enough sleep because of work obligations, family life, parenting, physical pain, and other demands.

In fact, a recent study found that adults with regular and adequate sleep had a 39 percent lower risk of death than those with irregular and insufficient sleep. Of course, this does not mean that everyone needs to have the exact same bedtime every night. However, getting enough sleep and maintaining a relatively consistent sleep schedule are reasonable parts of taking care of your health.

5. Maintain Relationships and Purpose

Longevity is not only about physical health. As humans, we are social beings, and meaningful relationships can play an important role in our well-being.

This does not necessarily mean we need to be around people all the time. What matters is having meaningful connections with others and feeling that we belong somewhere. Those connections can provide support, purpose, and a sense of belonging, which can become especially important as we age. Our relationships and sense of purpose can influence not only how long we live but also how we experience our lives as we get older.

How to Approach Longevity in a Practical Way

If you want to take your long-term health seriously, start with the areas that are most likely to have a meaningful impact.

  1. Think about what matters to you. Think about what you want your health to allow you to do as you get older. Also, try to be realistic about what you can and can not control. We can’t control everything about how we age or whether we develop certain health conditions. But knowing why your health matters to you can help you decide what changes are worth making.

  2. Take physical functioning seriously. As much as possible, intentionally find ways to maintain cardiovascular fitness, strength, mobility, and muscle as you age. If you are new to physical activity, start small. Trying to change too much at once can make it harder to stick with a new routine. The goal is to build habits you can maintain over time.

  3. Recognize your important health markers. Talk with your healthcare provider about blood pressure, blood glucose, cholesterol, and other measures that are relevant to your health. If you feel anxious about getting a checkup, especially if it has been a while, that is totally normal. However, knowing where you stand can help you make informed decisions about your health.

  4. Prioritize sleep and invest in your relationships. Try to aim for enough sleep and a reasonably consistent sleep schedule. You do not need a perfect routine. Find something that works for your life and try to make it consistent. At the same time, attempt to make time for the people, activities, and communities that give your life connection and purpose.

Bottom Line

Living longer is only part of the conversation we should be having. What matters the most is being able to live those additional years in a way that allows you to do the things that matter most to you. You do not have to change everything at once. Instead, try to begin with where you are, focus on what you can control, and remember that there is always an opportunity to take another step toward living a healthier and more meaningful life.

item.title: Food for Thought: Making Choices That Reinforce Self-Discipline
item.description:
Health

Food for Thought: Making Choices That Reinforce Self-Discipline

Personal Perspective: For changes to occur, thoughts must become self-initiated actions.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Each day is a new day, and each day, choices are made.
  • Choices involve self-discipline.
  • Self-discipline is a thought and a desire; but it must be an action for change to take place.
Source: Tumisu / Pixabay

I am not a qualified dietitian. With this in mind, consider the following. My daily morning smoothie ritual includes honey, probiotic yogurt, chia seeds, flaxseed meal, wheat germ, and ginger mixed with water in a large cup, which I stir with a spoon to make the smoothie.

According to my research, the individual ingredients have potentially been associated with digestive health, gut microbiota support, fiber intake, and nutrient density. In this context, nutrient density refers to foods that provide a concentrated source of nutrients and bioactive compounds, including fiber, vitamins, minerals, omega-3 fatty acids, probiotics, and proteins, all of which may offer potential health benefits.

From my personal perspective, this ritual does produce feelings of satisfied well-being. As such, I enjoy both the ritual and the experience of having this smoothie (Al-Younis et al., 2025; Anh et al., 2020; Brandolini & Hidalgo, 2012; Chakma et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Kok & Hutkins, 2018; Naureen et al., 2022; Nowak & Jeziorek, 2023; Pasupuleti et al., 2017; Shim et al., 2024).

A tablespoon of probiotic yogurt apparently provides live, active probiotics (friendly bacteria) that may support the gut microbiome, which is considered to be beneficial for digestive health and perhaps even general well-being.

In relation to chia seeds and flaxseed meal, flaxseed meal is produced from crushed flaxseeds and is reported to provide alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), plant-based omega-3 fatty acids, dietary fiber, lignans, and other bioactive compounds that have been associated with potential health benefits.

Chia seeds also contribute ALA and fiber, while wheat germ provides vitamin E, zinc, magnesium, and B vitamins that are purported to be necessary for cellular repair and healthy metabolic function.

The fiber from wheat germ, chia seeds, and flaxseed meal in the digestive system may support what can be colloquially referred to as "keeping the plumbing pipes"—that is, the intestines—potentially "clean" and "smooth."

Complementing these effects, ginger contains gingerol, while honey contains compounds with reported antibacterial properties. Collectively, these ingredients have been associated with potential digestive and well-being benefits (Al-Younis et al., 2025; Anh et al., 2020; Brandolini & Hidalgo, 2012; Chakma et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Kok & Hutkins, 2018; Naureen et al., 2022; Nowak & Jeziorek, 2023; Pasupuleti et al., 2017; Shim et al., 2024).

Choices

Each day, choosing the ritual of preparing this blend reinforces commitment and that of self-discipline. Self-discipline is not a thought or a desire; it must be an action. For me, this ritual and action also reminds me of the reason for the following maxim: "You are what you eat."

To that, I add another maxim pertaining to exercise: “You are what you do.” When it comes to exercise, I aim to exercise every day. This can be as simple as a five-minute walk from the front gate and a five-minute walk back. This can be in the morning, evening, or any time, for that matter.

In relation to myself, my chosen and preferred exercise is the prescribed forms of Goju Karate. The maximum time I have in mind is 30 minutes, but at times 15 minutes is sufficient. This exercise program (irrespective of the choice of exercise) is what I refer to as mind and body well-being maintenance.

This personally chosen exercise-maintenance program is not equivalent to training for an elite sporting event. Whether the goal is personal maintenance or elite sporting performance, there is no mystery or magic in any of this; it’s all up to you and your choices, and at times, none of this is easy.

Source: Markus Winkler/Pixabay

Whenever I have the thought of not wanting to do any of this, this is when I self-reflectively and determinedly tell myself to begin. And even when this happens, it may still not be easy. However, at other times, when it is easy, well, it is easy.

When I complete the task (irrespective of whether it was difficult or easy), I always—and yes, always is the case—I always feel good about what I had just achieved.

And even with this good feeling in place, what happens next time (which may again be easy or difficult) all of this will again be determined by my choices.

This, for me, is the ebb and flow of life. Will any of this change the world? Nope! But it does change me.

"I am responsible for, and I have the power over what I think, do, say, learn and choose" (Purje, 2014).

item.title: Why Do You Feel What Someone Else Can’t?
item.description:
Emotions

Why Do You Feel What Someone Else Can’t?

Sometimes the emotion no one can express shows up in the person who overreacts.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Emotions can move through a family system; the overreacting person may be expressing something unspoken.
  • Triangulation can shift tension from one relationship onto another person.
  • Differentiation helps us stay connected without carrying emotions that aren’t ours.

It’s dinner time, and the family is gathered around the table. If you were a neighbour passing by the window, you wouldn’t notice anything unusual. Just a regular family, having a regular dinner. But underneath the surface, there are waves of emotions.

The mother who sits at the table is angry and hurt. She is tired, but she prefers to act normal, pass the salt, and make sure everyone is full before going to bed. She keeps eating, answering questions, and carrying on.

But suddenly, the youngest daughter of the family is breaking down in a tantrum. It looks like it came from nowhere. The other family members are looking at her; the attention shifts, and they are wondering: What just happened here? What made her snap in such a disproportionate way?

A psychological lens can provide us with a real clue: the mother is experiencing the distress, while the daughter is the one expressing it. This can happen in close relationships. Sometimes an emotion that one person is struggling to experience, express, or contain shows up somewhere else in the family.

Family therapist Murray Bowen studied this kind of emotional process.

Anxiety doesn't always stay with the person who feels it

The core idea behind the theory is that we are not emotionally separate from the people around us. Families function as emotional systems, and when tension rises in one person, it can move through relationships.

When two people are experiencing tension between them, they usually call in a third party to reduce the tension or shift the attention. This is what Bowen called triangulation.

It might be that there is an unspoken tension between the mother and the father at the dinner table. While the issue is not addressed directly, it is carried in the air. The daughter catches it, she becomes overwhelmed, and it is expressed as a breakdown.

She is not pretending. She might be the person whose nervous system is most visibly showing what the family as a whole is struggling to contain.

The emotional messenger

The daughter’s role in our story is to express the emotion that her mother is feeling but struggling to express. She becomes the emotional messenger.

The messenger is often the person in a family who is known as the emotional one: the child who suddenly falls apart (with “no good reason”), the teenager who is always angry, the anxious partner. It might be tempting to frame their emotional intensity as an individual problem, but it might not be the case. Sometimes the messenger is expressing something bigger, giving the emotions that flow through family relationships an outlet.

It can happen in friendships, too. A friend can insist that she is completely fine after a breakup, while you might feel unusually protective or angry at her ex. You care about your friend, of course, but it might also be emotional work that happens through you, while your friend is still unable to touch the pain and anger directly.

You haven’t volunteered to be the messenger and carry her feelings for her. You are not pretending; you actually feel all the feelings. You are expressing emotions that exist between the couple but haven’t found a way out. While emotions don’t tend to disappear, they do tend to find a person who is willing to carry them.

So what do you do with this?

Bowen's concept of differentiation of self is particularly relevant here. You don’t need to detach yourself from the emotional situation completely, but it might be helpful to recognize your own thoughts and feelings while staying emotionally connected to the people you care about.

Differentiation doesn't mean becoming detached or unaffected. It means being able to stay emotionally connected to the people you love while maintaining enough clarity to recognize your own thoughts and feelings.

The interesting question is what happens in the space between them, where one person's unspoken emotion becomes another person's visible distress.
