item.title: Medical Negligence or Psychiatric Malpractice?
item.description:
Psychiatry

Medical Negligence or Psychiatric Malpractice?

A fresh look at a landmark ruling that changed American psychiatry.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • The initial takeaway from Osheroff v. Chestnut Lodge was that drug treatment was superior to talk therapy.
  • The case found that psychoanalytic psychiatry should cease being an exclusive treatment option for inpatients.
  • New information about the case paints a far more complex picture.
Source: University of California Press / Used with permission

When Eric Caplan, a medical historian, visited someone close to him being treated for depression at McLean Hospital in Belmont, MA, in the early 2020s, next to the reception was a sign that read—“ECT and Ketamine”—with an arrow pointing the way.

Like many other psychiatric institutions across the United States, Caplan explains in When Healing Harms: The Doctor Who Put a Hospital on Trial—and the Case That Shook Psychiatry, published today by the University of California Press, “treatment for those with depression now focused almost exclusively on the brain—procedures, medications, neuromodulation—with little attention to the mind or person inhabiting it.”

It wasn’t always that way, least of all at McLean: “Once a bastion of psychoanalysis and psychotherapy, McLean had largely abandoned any attempt to alleviate the disorder through conversation.”

An End to the Talking-Cure?

The dwindling of treatment options to two such highly contested measures, electroconvulsive therapy and ketamine, each with track records documenting numerous short- and longer-term harms, owes much to the influence of a single legal case, Osheroff v. Chestnut Lodge.

Settled before trial in 1983, though quickly assuming the status of a landmark ruling, the case was widely debated in American psychiatry journals and at conferences. The settlement reached helped determine institutional liability and inpatient protocols for years, if not decades.

The case was meant to put Chestnut Lodge, a Maryland-based psychiatric hospital, on trial for not prescribing antidepressants and tranquilizers to Raphael (“Ray”) Osheroff, an MD and well-regarded kidney specialist. On the verge of a painful third divorce and an ugly custody battle from his second marriage, Osheroff had voluntarily checked himself in for inpatient treatment.

He was diagnosed with severe depression but also treated for a character disorder that at the time did not formally exist.

Diagnostic Battlelines

Caplan’s riveting re-examination of the case provides fresh information from exhaustive archival research and in-depth interviews. The result is an absorbing page-turner that recasts the stakes around medical ethics, making the case less about a simple binary between psychoanalysis and pharmacology, and more about the muddled gray areas and blind spots strongly implicating both.

Consider what we now know from Caplan’s re-analysis of the material:

  • Before checking himself into Chestnut Lodge, Osheroff had already been prescribed a tricyclic antidepressant (Sinequan) by the prominent biological psychiatrist Nathan Kline, to little positive effect.
  • The Lodge took that into consideration when determining its own treatment protocols.
  • The psychoanalytic psychiatrist (Francis Board) who had recommended the institution to Osheroff did so on the basis that its treatment would involve as little medication as possible.
  • The institution’s mostly drug-free protocol was widely known at the time among recommending psychiatrists.
Eric Caplan
Source: Noah Willman / Used with permission

In addition, Caplan notes, the effort by hospitals such as Chestnut Lodge to reduce and, where possible, avoid psychiatric drugs altogether aligned with widespread concern at the time about the safety and dependency-forming profile of first-generation antidepressants and, later, of the tricyclics prescribed in the 1960s and '70s.

By the early 1980s, during the same months Osheroff was an inpatient, problems of consent over the right to refuse medication led to the passage of legislation in Maine and 23 other states, guaranteeing medical refusal rights to all psychiatric patients, voluntary or involuntary. Separately, Colorado began allowing voluntary, involuntary, and competent patients to refuse psychotropic medication, unless they presented an immediate risk to themselves or others.

Diagnosis: Mistreatment

During the litigation, conflicts came to light at the Lodge that helped speed the settlement in Osheroff’s favor:

  • Approval of an MHPG urine test by one of his doctors (Dingman) without consultation with the patient’s primary therapist (Ross), suggesting concern about progress on psychotherapy alone.
  • The plaintiff daily paced the ward for hours, his feet blackened and blistered. Osheroff was disheveled and mumbling, yet had entered the institution clean-cut, wearing a business suit.
  • His therapist’s rigid adherence to the work of Otto F. Kernberg included the notion of “restructuring” Osheroff’s personality to exclude a previously defining character disorder. That made his depression secondary, but also symptomatic.
  • Osheroff was treated on the basis of draft criteria for a disorder that wasn’t yet bona fide.

Was Osheroff’s Treatment Psychoanalytic?

Whenever Dr. Osheroff asked if he could leave the Lodge—and he did so repeatedly—he was told (according to Ross’s therapy notes), “When you develop a decent fantasy about yourself.”

Osheroff needed years-long treatment, allegedly, because he was “symbolically dead” and would otherwise “disappear off the face of the earth.” The form and style of Kernberg’s applied transference-focused psychotherapy (TFP) was alternately taunting and punitive, bullying and cruel. “You are a patriarch? Ha, ha … You’re merely pathetic—crazy on the inside, sane on the outside. Take a tin cup and go beg on Connecticut Avenue.”

Board, Osheroff’s longtime psychoanalytic psychiatrist before and after, worried about worse outcomes from a patient pushed to such extremes: the “badgering and destructive superego” was more likely to result in “precisely the opposite of the appropriate type of treatment” needed, he remarked, making the approach not just “ill-advised” but also expressive of an “unconscious sadism,” in that it would almost certainly deepen the doctor’s suffering.

Pharmacology—or a Different Psychotherapy—to the Rescue?

With the aid of his parents, Osheroff was moved from Chestnut Lodge to Silver Hill Hospital in Connecticut, where, from a sympathetic, differently oriented psychoanalytic psychiatrist (Joan Narad), he was briefly prescribed Elavil (amitriptyline) for depression and Thorazine (chlorpromazine) for agitation, with accompanying psychotherapy that was designed to be reparative, not destructive.

Osheroff recovered with sufficient strength to return to work. Once there, he would confront and eventually litigate the profound treachery of his business associates, who tried to take all of his clients while he was in hospital and, ultimately, take over the dialysis center itself.

Later estranged from his third wife, though briefly buoyed by the Lodge’s financial settlement of his case, as by victory over his colleagues, his depression returned, indicating the drugs he had been prescribed were at best a temporary, short-term aid.

Conclusions: Mistreatment and Institutional Failure

Amid all this legal and psychiatric drama, with the case assuming field-wide significance, Caplan captures the frustration and desperation of its central protagonist, initially flailing at the rigidity of an institution that, in its own assessment, wanted to “restructure” his personality, whatever damage that entailed.

“Where supportive psychotherapy should have focused on helping [Osheroff] clarify immediate struggles and find adaptive responses,” Caplan concludes, Ross’s “confrontational method” at the Lodge “only intensified his already fragile self-criticism.”

Though Osheroff v. Chestnut Lodge was widely assumed to cement biological psychiatry as preferable to psychotherapy, with less liability, When Healing Harms paints a far more complex picture. Serious errors are made on all sides, victory is largely mischaracterized, and an ambitious, obsessive doctor is left craving vindication years later.

item.title: The Death Penalty and Brain Impairment
item.description:
Punishment

The Death Penalty and Brain Impairment

Another reason to oppose capital punishment.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Brain damage, especially Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD), is found in many condemned prisoners.
  • Psychologists, and other forensic experts, tend to miss or give insufficient weight to FASD.
  • The tragic case of Christa Pike, whose execution was recently botched, illustrates this problem.

In 2013, I penned a post for Psychology Today titled “A Foolish and Barbaric Practice: Seven Reasons to Oppose Capital Punishment.” The seven reasons I cited were: (1) unequal administration (die in Phoenix, live in Tucson; die if poor or have bad lawyers, live if rich or have good ones), (2) tremendous cost of litigation, (3) many post-conviction exonerations, (4) lack of evidence that it deters murder, (5) myth that it provides closure for victims’ families, (6) cruelty of being in a condemned state for years or decades and (7) change in moral consensus (many states have abolished capital punishment, and almost no other first-world nation still allows it).

At that time, I was in the process of moving from Colorado to California, but was able to get my post placed on the desk of Governor (today Senator) John Hickenlooper, who was considering whether or not to support a Bill that would bring Colorado (which had actually abolished it in 1900 but then brought it back a few years later) onto the growing list of states that have abolished capital punishment. Afterwards, Hickenlooper announced that he would not sign death warrants for any of the three prisoners at that time on Colorado’s death row and listed most of my seven reasons.

Both before and after I published my post, I served as a forensic expert in many death penalty proceedings, typically over the question of possible Intellectual Disability (ID, formerly known as Mental Retardation). As a result of my experience with people accused or convicted of murder, if I was writing the post today, I would add an eighth reason. In fact, I plan to write a small book titled “America’s Shame: Eight Reasons to Oppose Capital Punishment.” My eighth reason is that an extremely large percentage of people who commit murders have diagnosed, or diagnosable, brain-based developmental conditions that produce cognitive limitations which reduce, even if they do not eliminate, degree of criminal responsibility. (I should point out that “reduce” is a relative term, as even for offenders found to have ID, a usual substitute for the death penalty is life without possibility of parole, a punishment considered so severe that it is banned by the European Union.

An Early Claim of Offender Brain Impairment

Starting in the 1970s, the claim that brain impairment is commonplace among death row inhabitants was made in publications by Yale forensic psychiatrist Dorothy Otnow Lewis and her colleague, Georgetown neurologist Jonathan Pincus. According to the (now 93-year-old) Lewis, there are three factors that characterize the vast majority of violent criminals: (1) extremely abusive upbringings; (2) psychiatric symptomatology, such as paranoia, and (c) neurological impairment.

With respect to this third factor, Lewis studied death row inhabitants around the U.S. and claimed to find overt signs of brain damage (such as abnormal EEG’s) in virtually all of them. Dr. Lewis’ work was not without controversy, however, as her claims regarding brain damage were challenged on methodological grounds by other experts. Some of this criticism likely reflected experts’ unwillingness to admit that they might have “missed the boat” in their own reports or testimony.

Missing Fetal Alcohol Exposure

Lewis’ research was conducted before many of the powerful diagnostic tools (such as brain scans) in widespread use today were available. The biggest problem with her work, however, was more conceptual than methodological, and it had to do with her main focus being on traumatic brain injury rather than a more common (and usually much more devastating) form of brain damage. I am talking specifically about Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD), which noted forensic psychologist Dr. Natalie Novick Brown, among many others, has shown to be a very common cause of frontal lobe dysfunction in people accused of committing violent crimes.

Lewis’ oversight is understandable in that FASD (then termed FAS) was not written about in a medical journal until 1973 and did not become widely known and used for several decades after that. FASD is caused entirely by excessive consumption of alcohol by a pregnant woman and is the main reason for the warnings posted in liquor stores and bars throughout the United States. Even today, at a time when FASD is much better known, the majority of forensic experts miss it entirely, and even when it is noted, it is typically given little if any weight.

The Tragic Case of Christa Pike

An example of this can be found in the recent botched execution in Tennessee of Christa Pike. At the time of this writing, Ms. Pike (who resided on death row in Nashville for 31 years) is clinging to life after two failed administrations of a usually lethal chemical. In 1995, when she was in the Job Corps, then 18-year-old Pike—along with her 17-year-old boyfriend—stabbed and slashed to death another Job Corps resident, 19-year-old Coleen Slemmer. Pike, who became a suspect by blabbing about the crime, quickly gave a full confession when interrogated.

The focus of forensic testimony about Ms. Pike, as well as legal efforts to save her, has been almost entirely on her horrendous family environment (such as years-long sexual abuse beginning when she was a toddler) and serious emotional problems (such as a suicide attempt at age 12). The possibility of brain damage was never given much emphasis, either by forensic experts (one defense expert actually testified that she could not have brain damage, pointing to her full-scale IQ score of 111). In fact, there were many indicators of brain damage, including multiple seizures starting in infancy, substantial exposure to alcohol in utero (and a diagnosis of FASD), plus a serious birth complication.

A compilation of expert reports posted by Cornell’s Center for the Death Penalty Worldwide illustrates the problem of “diagnostic overshadowing.” An example of this occurs when psychiatric symptoms are so extreme that less salient but more explanatory factors, such as blatant evidence of brain impairment, are overlooked. To me, the most shocking example of that can be seen in a 2001 report about Christa Pike by Dr. Jonathan Pincus, the forensic neurologist who had been a pioneer with Dorothy Otnow Lewis in bringing attention to the frequency of brain damage in condemned prisoners. In his report, Dr. Pincus focused only on Christa Pike’s Bipolar Disorder and history of horrific abuse, and said not a word about her prenatal alcohol exposure and many other indications of neurological impairment. Among the reasons why this is unfortunate is that courts and juries tend to give little weight to even extreme forms of the “abuse excuse,” while brain damage, especially when it first manifests in babies, is more likely to elicit sympathy, even for offenders who go on to commit awful crimes.

item.title: Beyond 'Yes': Why the Process of Consent Matters
item.description:
Education

Beyond 'Yes': Why the Process of Consent Matters

Rethinking consent through context, autonomy, and reasonable belief.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • When consent is seen as a box-ticking exercise, the genuine wishes of the other person can be overlooked.
  • It's vital to establish that both parties are freely choosing to participate and have capacity to do so.
  • Thinking critically about how consent was obtained takes it beyond simply getting a "yes."

For decades, consent education has emphasised two simple principles: No means no, and sexual activity requires a voluntary and informed "yes." Yet recently reported behaviour from college campuses raises an uncomfortable question. What if some individuals are hearing that message very differently? What if, instead of viewing consent as a way of understanding another person's wishes, they merely view it as a hurdle to overcome before they’re able to get on with what they actually want to do? Under this mindset, the focus shifts away from whether the other person genuinely wants the sexual activity and moves toward securing just enough agreement to proceed.

This is a dangerous perspective. When the objective becomes to obtain a "yes" by whatever means possible, persistence, pressure, intoxication, emotional manipulation, social obligation, or exploiting vulnerability can all become part of the process (Kubota & Nakazawa, 2024). Once some form of agreement is secured, however compromised, it can be wrongly viewed as a green light not only for the act in question but also for any behaviour that follows.

When sexual assaults happen, people often assume that the perpetrator was told no and chose to ignore it. While this is sometimes the case, the uncomfortable reality is that many perpetrators are aware of the need to get some kind of yes, and actively work to obtain something, anything, that can later be pointed to as consent. In this context, the perpetrator's attention is not directed toward understanding the wishes of the other person. It’s directed toward obtaining what they want. The victim becomes increasingly irrelevant to them, except as the means through which that goal is achieved.

What does this mean for consent education?

The lesson here is not that consent education is unnecessary—quite the opposite, in fact. However, these cases suggest that some aspects of consent education may require rethinking. Many educational programmes focus on behavioural rules to follow to gain consent, such as checking in with the other person, listening for them saying yes, and accepting it when they say no (Koenigsberg, 2024). These messages are important and well-intentioned. However, it may be that some people are interpreting the rules in different ways. While the aim of the messaging is usually "make sure the other person genuinely wants this," someone who is focused primarily on their own desires may hear something quite different. They hear, "I need evidence of consent before I proceed." The difference between these two interpretations is subtle but profound.

One solution is for consent education within schools, colleges, and universities to devote more attention to the conditions under which agreement emerges. Rather than asking students simply whether consent was obtained, educators should encourage them to think critically about how that consent came about. Was the other person enthusiastic, or merely going along with the situation? Were they making a free and informed choice, or responding to pressure, social obligation, intoxication, fear of awkwardness, or a desire to avoid conflict? Most importantly, training should shift the focus beyond "How do I get consent?" toward "How do I know the other person genuinely wants this?" This requires individuals to think about consent in the context of empathy, perspective-taking, and respect for the other person's autonomy, rather than seeing it as merely a box to be ticked.

How does this align with the law?

Interestingly, this approach is already reflected in the law in some countries. For example, under the U.K. Sexual Offences Act (2003), those accused of sexual offences are required to demonstrate that they held a reasonable belief that the other person consented, including outlining what steps they took to establish whether consent was present. In other words, the law doesn’t simply ask whether someone believed they had consent. It asks whether it was reasonable for them to have that belief. This distinction is important because it shifts attention away from the mere existence of agreement and toward the process through which it emerged. Ultimately, the goal should not be producing individuals who know how to secure a "yes" but individuals who care whether that "yes" reflects a genuine desire to participate.

Beyond consent education

At this point, it’s important to acknowledge that not every perpetrator who commits sexual violence is working from a flawed understanding of consent. Some know exactly what’s OK and what’s not, yet they still choose to disregard this. Why? Because they want to. Maybe they’ve done it before, and nothing happened, so they feel emboldened to keep doing it, or even to make it part of the social norms within their group or fraternity. For these individuals, the problem is not a failure to understand consent but a willingness to prioritise their own sexual gratification over another person's autonomy, dignity, and well-being. Therefore, prevention cannot rely on education alone. Universities, colleges, and wider society must also be willing to hold individuals accountable when they exploit intoxication, vulnerability, coercion, or social pressure for their own benefit. Education may help those who misunderstand consent, but accountability is needed for those who understand it and simply do not care.

item.title: Anxiety and Loneliness Have a Surprising Remedy
item.description:
Mindfulness

Anxiety and Loneliness Have a Surprising Remedy

Using mindful self-massage to calm your nervous system.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Massage therapist Raphael Lavoie-Brand developed mindful self-massage during the COVID-19 lockdowns.
  • Mindful self-massage pairs gentle touch with mindfulness and self-compassion.
  • With daily practice, people report better sleep, less stress and tension, and a kinder view of their bodies.
  • The technique works best with attention to pleasant sensations and an intention of kindness toward yourself.

I recently sat down with Raphael Lavoie-Brand, a massage therapist who developed an approach to mindful self-massage during the pandemic. He teaches it to help people relieve stress and anxiety, sleep better, and build a kinder relationship with themselves. Up until now, it has only been taught in French. After our first conversation, I saw its potential as a somatic practice almost anyone can use, one that combines the benefits of massage with self-compassion work. Raphael also created an English-language video preview of his technique exclusively for this page.

Annie Chen: What is mindful self-massage?

Raphael Lavoie-Brand: It's a touch-based approach to calm our nervous system, relax our body, and improve our relationship with ourselves. It combines effortless self-massage techniques with mindfulness and self-compassion.

For example, slow hand movements can be paired with awareness of breath, gratitude practices, or savoring pleasant sensations. One could say it is a movement meditation that enhances self-care through quality touch.

AC: When did you realize self-massage could be a powerful form of healing?

RLB: During the early COVID lockdowns, I was worried about the high levels of loneliness, stress, and anxiety. Teaching self-massage online seemed like a way to help.

One day I was experimenting with self-massage and mindfulness while very stressed and exhausted. For the first time, the therapeutic touch I gave clients became fully accessible to my own body. Mindfulness opened the door for me to give and receive high-quality touch simultaneously, in a profoundly soothing way.

Later, students who practiced daily told me their mood, sleep, and stress management improved, and their self-love grew. They were surprised to have this impact with their own hands.

AC: Who can benefit most?

RLB: People who struggle with stress, anxiety, loneliness, sleep difficulties, grief, illness, body image issues, muscle tension, and some digestive discomforts. Those who see concrete benefits practice daily, at least 5 to 10 minutes.

One woman with long-time anxiety and insomnia went through a breakup and retired at the same time. Self-massage helped her fall asleep faster and stay calm when she was awake at night. Over time, she slept much better and felt relieved chronic neck tension.

Many people with ADHD also tell me it makes meditation accessible when sitting still seems impossible.

AC: Is it possible to go through the motions and still miss the psychological benefit?

RLB: Absolutely. Doing the motions automatically while thinking about your to-do list is not effective. It is about attention and intention. Attention is what we receive through our awareness. We choose to focus on pleasant sensations, also called savoring, which has proven benefits for stress reduction and happiness. Intention is what we give through touch: kindness, gratitude, a nonjudgmental mindset, and inner warmth. These attitudes toward our body are not intuitive in our culture, so we practice specific exercises to nurture them.

Together, attention and intention amount to a caring presence.

AC: Many people find it easier to be physically nurturing toward others than toward themselves. How do you work with that?

RLB: As mammals, we evolved to build attachment by physically nurturing our close ones, so it's normal to find caring touch easier to offer others. To paraphrase Kristin Neff, that's good news: We already have an instinctual resource to care for others, and we can mirror it back to ourselves. Instead of building compassion from the ground up, we work on a bridge. I use "quality of touch" exercises with visualization, movement, and self-touch to create it.

AC: Is there research supporting the benefits you've observed anecdotally?

RLB: Three recent studies inspired by mindful self-compassion found that short, daily self-soothing touch practices could reduce cortisol, perceived stress, fatigue, and loneliness. A controlled study in France found that a 10-minute bedtime self-massage improved sleep duration and depth after four weeks. A 2023 systematic review reported self-massage studies showing improvements in anxiety, sleep, depressive symptoms, and pain.

AC: Loneliness is a growing public health concern. Can self-massage help?

RLB: I think it can soothe the distress of loneliness and help replace unhealthy cravings that form when people are too lonely. Part of being lonely is lacking affective touch, and self-massage adds a layer of care that combines physical and psychological effects.

Co-regulation with other human beings is still probably the best solution, but even online, live groups create connection, which especially helps people who find it hard to leave home because of health or age.

AC: How can self-massage help people whose relationship with touch is complicated by trauma?

RLB: When someone is uncomfortable with touch, self-massage offers an experience that is fully under your control. Duration, body regions, and frequency are easy to adapt.

I once massaged someone recovering from touch aversion due to trauma, and the one-hour session itself was a trigger. Small doses would have been better, which is hard to do with traditional massage.

Mindful self-massage could be compatible with body-based somatic therapy, for example, as a take-home practice.

AC: Does consent play a role in self-massage?

RLB: Yes. Touch is being instructed by a person of "authority," and participants with a compliant personality may feel estranged from their own touch if they follow along without agency. Some may even be triggered, especially those with past trauma or body image issues. This is why I invite participants to prioritize their comfort and feel free to participate or not at all times. They are welcome to change, adapt, cease, or skip any movement for any reason. They can also choose to just watch instead.

In healthcare settings or at corporate wellness days, it should only be offered on a voluntary basis. Unlike stretching, touch is quite intimate.

AC: How can this practice improve someone's relationships with others?

RLB: Quality touch can reassure a patient before surgery, help a baby fall asleep, console a person without words, and make intimacy more enjoyable. Self-massage can also improve body image, making it easier to connect physically with a partner.

One woman's growing awareness of touch let her connect with her dying mother through mutual caresses of their hands, when her mother could no longer speak. Long after her mother passed, she said she felt an imprint of her mother's love in her hands, which helped her grieve.

Raphael Lavoie-Brand
Source: Raphael Lavoie-Brand / Used with permission

AC: Some of my clients struggle with sleep and loneliness in the middle of the night. Is there a practice that could help?

RLB: Yes. I produced a video specially for Psychology Today's audience. It is a two-part video with a sleep routine in the second part. It can be done lying down or sitting. [Click here for the full video.]

AC: What would a beginner's first week look like?

RLB: Most beginners see encouraging improvements within a week of daily 10-minute practice, simply following my videos or live sessions.

In the first week, it's good to try techniques for different needs: neck and shoulders, digestive comfort, morning activation, or bedtime. Then choose one or two routines to integrate into daily life. You'll gradually memorize the movements and feel the deepening effects of repetition.

Learn more about Raphael Lavoie-Brand's work on his website, in English or French.
